target: AG1’s claim that alternative energies can effectively replace fossil-fuel electricity because some countries already run on very high renewable shares
objection: High-renewable countries like Iceland, Paraguay, Costa Rica, and Norway are special cases and do not prove that alternative energy can replace fossil fuels across large, diverse energy systems; the United States, for example, has never historically exceeded 20% alternative-energy use.

target: AG1’s broader claim that fossil fuels can be replaced overall by alternative energy
objection: Replacing fossil fuels requires more than decarbonizing electricity; it must also cover transport fuels, building heating, and industrial/process heat, which remain major fossil-fuel uses.

target: AG1’s reliance on nuclear as a quick replacement strategy
objection: Nuclear power is too dangerous and ineffective to be a serious solution to global warming, with accidents such as Fukushima erasing carbon-free electricity gains, so a rapid nuclear-based transition is not robust.

target: AG2’s objection that fossil-fuel replacement must include non-electric uses and that electricity alone is insufficient
objection: Alternative-energy pathways can cover transport, heating, and industrial heat: transport can use electric vehicles, buildings can use heat pumps, and industry can use electrification or renewable-derived hydrogen for higher-temperature needs.

target: AG2’s assumption that variable renewables cannot support reliable fossil-fuel replacement
objection: Although renewable electricity is variable, grid interconnections, energy storage, and flexible demand can smooth that variability enough to support reliable power for end uses.

target: AG1’s claim that renewables plus grid tools can provide reliable power for electrified end uses
objection: Grid interconnections, storage, and flexible demand have practical limits in duration, capacity, and their ability to cover long low-generation periods for a whole large system, so alternative electricity alone cannot reliably provide firm year-round power.

target: AG1’s implication that electrifying transport and heating does not fundamentally worsen the reliability problem
objection: Electrifying transport and heating raises electricity demand, including seasonal heating loads and peak transportation demand, so effective fossil-fuel replacement would require continuous firm electricity supply that alternatives cannot guarantee by themselves.

target: AG2’s claim that dispatchable fossil generation is still needed because renewables are intermittent
objection: A low-carbon system can include nuclear power, which provides firm, dispatchable electricity rather than intermittent-only output, so reliability does not require dispatchable fossil generation.

target: AG1’s claim that nuclear can cover low-renewable periods and peaks fast enough to remove fossil backup
objection: Nuclear cannot be treated as instantly scalable continuous firm power because build-out, construction timelines, maintenance/refueling, and outage risks limit how quickly it can supply enough reliable capacity across a large economy.

target: AG2’s claim that natural gas as a bridge is necessary because high-renewable systems still need fossil backup
objection: Countries such as Iceland, Paraguay, Costa Rica, and Norway already operate power systems with very high renewable electricity shares, which suggests that reliability does not inherently require an ongoing natural-gas bridge as a general rule.

target: AG2’s claim that nuclear is the only main firm low-carbon option
objection: High-renewable electricity systems can also draw firm, dispatchable low-carbon power from non-nuclear sources such as hydro and geothermal, so nuclear is not the sole main candidate for firm capacity.

target: AG2’s claim that alternative energy systems still need natural gas as an unavoidable bridge
objection: A portfolio of renewables, nuclear firming, grid interconnections, storage, and flexible demand can provide reliable low-carbon electricity, so dispatchable fossil backup is not inherently required.

target: AG2’s assumption that only nuclear can provide firm low-carbon power and that nuclear timing therefore determines whether fossil backup is needed
objection: The countries with very high renewable electricity shares include inherently firm renewable sources such as hydro and geothermal, showing that firm low-carbon power can come from non-nuclear alternatives as well.

target: AG1’s claim that hydro/geothermal can substitute for nuclear-scale firm capacity
objection: Hydro is constrained by hydrology, water availability, and reservoir operations, while geothermal is geographically limited; because of these constraints, they cannot be assumed to scale rapidly to provide nationwide all-season firm capacity in large, diverse energy systems.

target: AG1’s broader conclusion that alternative-energy portfolios alone can provide reliable fossil-fuel replacement
objection: If firm low-carbon capacity from alternatives is not sufficient or rapidly scalable, system reliability still requires dispatchable generation during shortages, so alternatives alone cannot effectively replace fossil fuels at the needed scale and timing.

target: AG1’s overall claim that alternatives can replace fossil fuels in practice on a large-system basis
objection: Fossil fuels provide not just electricity but also high-density transport fuels and direct thermal/process heat, and simply scaling wind and solar electricity does not by itself reproduce those end-use energy services.

target: AG1’s implicit assumption that end-use conversion can happen quickly enough to make alternative energy a practical full replacement
objection: Replacing fossil fuels requires major transformations in vehicle fleets, industrial equipment, and fuel-conversion infrastructure, and those equipment and infrastructure changes are slow and time-consuming.

target: AG1’s assumption that alternatives can cover the transition period without ongoing fossil use
objection: Because end-use turnover and fuel-conversion infrastructure buildout are gradual, alternatives cannot rapidly supply all fossil-fuel energy services at the needed scale and timing during the transition.

target: AG1’s conclusion that fossil fuels are unnecessary once alternatives are pursued
objection: If alternatives cannot rapidly supply all fossil-fuel energy services during the transition, then fossil fuels remain necessary to maintain energy continuity and industrial and transport reliability.

target: AG1’s claim that natural gas is not needed as a bridge
objection: Natural gas can be deployed quickly using existing generation and industrial infrastructure, allowing faster emissions reductions than waiting for all low-carbon replacements and conversion infrastructure to scale, so it remains a necessary bridge fuel.
